newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss to vote Sunday on banning arms exports.
newsitem.headline: Swiss to vote Sunday on banning arms exports.

text.p: Swiss voters decide on Sunday whether to ban arms exports and the financing of the international weapons trade, abandoning a business that has at times put Switzerland in a harsh historic spotlight.

The government, parliament and industry have urged Swiss voters to reject the initiative, launched by the Social Democrats in 1992, as a misguided attempt at peace-making that could cost as many as 120,000 jobs in a lengthy recession.
But proponents say the measure, the subject of a referendum in Switzerland's system of direct democracy, will help shift the emphasis away from waging war and toward social development.

They hope the recent release of archives showing the bulk of Swiss arms exports during World War Two went to Nazi Germany and its then fascist ally Italy will encourage the Swiss to support the cause.

"Approval of this initiative would have serious consequences for our exporters," the government -- a coalition which includes two Social Democratic ministers -- said in its official comment on the proposal.
"The arms industry, which is dependent on exports, would be hit hardest, but broad segments of the civilian export industry would also be affected."
Not only would many jobs be jeopardised, but national defence, which relies on the products and know-how of Swiss industry, would be increasingly dependent on foreigners, the statement added.

The government, whose seven members have to accept majority decisions, agreed arms exports need special treatment because of their sensitive nature, but said existing rules were enough to keep Swiss weapons out of the wrong hands.
Swiss arms exports, which totalled 232.9 million Swiss francs ($166 million) in 1996, on average make up 0.5 to 1.0 percent of the world total, according to government figures.
Captains of industry are more concerned that the ban would also apply to so-called dual-use items like computers that have both military and civilian applications.
If the proposal is approved, these exports would be allowed only if the buyer gave assurances they would not be used for military purposes.
A defence ministry spokesman said Switzerland ranked fourth in the world in the export of such dual-use items.
Champions of the initiative have promoted their cause in moral terms.
"Arms deliveries always help contribute to destabilising the importing region and to militarising conflicts," the organising committee for the campaign that led to the calling of the referendum said.

"Arms deliveries reduce the chances for political and non-violent conflict resolution and fuel regional arms races. The price that humanity pays daily for the arms trade is out of all proportion to the intended use."

Swiss historian Mauro Cerutti, a researcher who studied Swiss diplomatic archives, said last month that Nazi Germany took nearly two-thirds of Swiss exports of arms and war material from 1940 to 1944.

The Germans received arms worth 600 million Swiss francs at the time. Fascist Italy took another 150 million francs worth of arms out of total wartime exports of 900 million. The dollar was worth around four Swiss francs at the war's end.
The Swiss also sold arms and war material to the Allies, but in smaller amounts.
